title: I Posted the Cotton-Candy Bowl Hours After They Took My Numbered Cone Rack

parts.text: I stepped into the sugar booth at 1:08 p.m. and host Trix was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE BOWL. THIRTY MINUTES. CONES STAY WITH THE SLOT. I was twenty-four, fair secretary, holding a clipboard that listed our numbered cone rack. Trix shrugged. "Hosts are the sugar." I photographed the board, the booking, and her leftover floss on my numbered cone rack. Then I asked for the bowl log. At 1:16 the booth pinged why Trix's name was on my floss. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The booth can see Trix's leftover floss on my numbered cone rack.

social.video_title: They took my numbered cotton-candy cone rack — Part 1/2
social.description: Sugar booth, leftover floss, a thirty-minute clock she posted. I logged the cones. Would you have asked for the bowl log?

parts.text: Trix called it spin-up until the booth asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the floss still. The cone rack went back to my numbered slot. Trix ran a slot of her own and told the next host atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: HOSTS ARE NOT THE SUGAR. I keep my cones on a labeled peg. Trix brown-bags her spin-up. The booth finally looks like a slot, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Hosts are not the sugar — Part 2/2
social.description: Bowl log, numbered cone rack, and a second line on the board. Was spin-up ever my floss?
